results.title: Everyone in the AI build is selling the same option to a different buyer
highlights:
Nebius, which raised its price while the market fell.

On 17 September, Nebius told customers that selected pay-as-you-go GPU rates rise 17% to 21% on 1 October. H100 goes from $3.85 to $4.50 an hour, H200 from $4.50 to $5.40, B200 from $7.15 to $8.50 and B300 from $7.85 to $9.50. By the 19th, the executed market went the other way. H100 was $2.85 versus $3.02 the day before and H200 was $5.13 versus $5.60. The new H100 card is 57.9% above the latest executed price.

I do not think that makes the list price useless though. Nebius still publishes preemptible rates of $2.15 for H100 and $2.45 for H200, and says a large multi-month reservation can get up to 35% off. Same accelerator, three prices. The fully flexible one is the one getting more expensive. You pay more if you want to turn up whenever you like.

...

If the preemptible rates stay where they are, the on-demand premium on H100 goes from $1.70 to $2.35 an hour. B300 goes from $3.55 to $5.20. Nebius has not published future preemptible rates, so I am holding those flat for now. The price increase lands on the customer who refuses to commit.

...

On 18 September, Duke Energy asked customers across the Carolinas to cut usage between 2 and 8 p.m. during a heat-driven peak. The next day, the Department of Energy used emergency authority to secure the same grid, including backup generation as a last resort, and said more than 35 GW of unused backup generation exists nationally. FERC is already running a rulemaking for large loads above roughly 20 MW, including faster connections for customers that can cut load when the grid is stressed. The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3, pushing more of the grid bill back onto large loads.

A data center that can switch off for a few hours may get connected sooner or pay less. The utility gets permission to cut the load when the grid is tight. For a project waiting on power, a few months saved on the connection can be worth more than a slightly cheaper power bill.

...

At the softer executed prices, H100 one-year economic carry goes from -12.2% to -14.7%, a 253bp hit from the rental price alone. H200 goes from 35.7% to 29.1%. At 70% leverage, H100 goes from -57.8% to -66.3% and H200 goes from 102.0% to 79.9%. SOFR did nothing because the last fixing was still Thursday’s 3.85%.

Nothing changed in the contract. Yesterday a three-year H100 commitment at $2.04 sat slightly below the base curve and hurt modeled carry. After the market softened, the same $2.04 gives about 166bp of protection. H200’s two-year mark gives about 402bp. The contract got more valuable because the market moved down around it.

...

Three of those six changes are basically a Saturday problem. Frontier demand, GPU supply and custom silicon went from up to flat because there were no new corporate filings. Nothing in the evidence says demand or supply actually softened.

Data-center power went from tight to worse after the Department of Energy stepped into the Carolinas. That is the first time this row got worse because of reliability rather than a longer queue. Macro went from worse to flat because the 10-year did nothing over the weekend. Older-GPU residuals went from improving to firm because price support held while the executed market underneath it softened.

Yesterday the bad rows were split between time and money. Today three of the four are physical: power, time to power and grid constraints. Depreciation is the only one that stayed bad on both days. Demand did not break. The pressure just moved back toward the physical side.

results.title: The GPU Already Lost This Job Once · Josef Chen
highlights:
CoreWeave raised $8.5 billion of debt in March to buy more GPUs. And if CoreWeave can't rent them all out? No worries. Under an order form it filed with the SEC last September, "NVIDIA is obligated to purchase the residual unsold capacity through April 13, 2032".

...

In January 2026 NVIDIA agreed to buy another $2 billion of CoreWeave equity. CoreWeave's $8.5bn of investment-grade debt in March, priced at SOFR+2.25% with final maturity in 2032, was underwritten against customer contracts that run as long as the loan. In August, the company priced a five-year loan for $2.6bn that's below investment grade and is priced SOFR+5.50%. CoreWeave's customer contracts there match an average duration of three years.

This circularity reminds me of Hashnest at a smaller scale. Under a $6.3 billion order form filed with the SEC back in September 2025, "NVIDIA is obligated to purchase the residual unsold capacity through April 13, 2032". As the August press release notes:

> By financing these shorter-date commitments, lenders are signalling confidence in the long-term value of NVIDIA GPUs running on CoreWeave's cloud platform and a willingness to underwrite renewal risk.

This can go badly without demand falling at all. The August loan has a five-year maturity, but the contracts average only three years. In 2029, if GPU rental rates don't cover the debt payments, whoever financed the GPUs has to sell into whatever the market is at the time; they can't sit tight and hope things work out. And if lots of leveraged GPU owners hold the same paper, it isn't a gradual GPU market decline but a steep one.

...

I do find it remarkable that a GPU could stay relevant for nine years. We seem to be betting the farm on H100 rental prices staying elevated for a very long time. The H100 rental index is down 57% in under three years (one-year rates are 38% off the October lows, but supply is constrained, with availability booked out since February). Across the industry, the bet that the debt gets repaid is a bet that GPUs will still be generating meaningful rental revenue nine years down the track. Happy to be wrong on that, but it's not a certainty to my mind.

results.title: GPU allocation pressure is repricing the entire AI infrastructure buy — The Spend Ledger
highlights:
Huawei said this week that demand for its AI chips is outpacing supply, and Reuters reported that on September 17. The polite reading is that the market is healthy. The correct reading is that the pricing mechanism has changed: buyers are no longer just negotiating rate, they are competing for position in an allocation queue.

That distinction is worth spelling out. When supply is elastic, procurement is a price problem. When supply is rationed, it becomes a sequencing problem, and the cost of being wrong is not a higher invoice but a longer wait and a worse fallback.

...

A September 15 analysis of Nvidia's Vera Rubin rack economics put a number on what concentrated supply actually means at the line-item level. In a VR200 NVL72 rack with a bill of materials running roughly $4 million, approximately 70% of that figure is attributed to the Rubin GPUs alone, excluding high-bandwidth memory.

That single figure explains the budget exposure better than any trend description could. When seven-tenths of a rack's cost sits in one component, any tightening in that component's availability transmits immediately into the whole procurement plan. The buyer cannot offset a GPU constraint by shopping around on memory or switching networking vendors. The expensive part is the part with the least substitution.

This is precisely why deal structure has started to function as part of the product. Long-term agreements, priority allocation windows, and vendor-backed capacity reservations are spreading not because vendors invented a new sales tactic but because rationing makes terms enforceable in a way that list pricing never was. The supplier with allocation power can demand take-or-pay commitments, advance payments, or cloud-mediated access. Buyers who cannot meet those terms move down the queue.

...

The practical implication for CFOs is direct. GPU pricing is not commodity pricing, and treating it that way produces budgets that are technically accurate on price-per-chip and wrong on total delivered cost. A buyer who can pre-commit capacity, demonstrate power readiness, and accept vendor terms gets access. A buyer who cannot gets a longer wait and a more expensive fallback generation.

...

Older GPU generations are getting cheaper as frontier buyers chase the newest parts.

...

What is actually happening is a two-tier split. The scarcity premium is concentrating at the frontier end precisely because newest-generation GPUs have the least elastic supply and the most vendor leverage. The secondary market getting cheaper is a symptom of that bifurcation, not a counterweight to it. Buyers who can accept older generations gain real savings. Buyers who cannot find the premium at the top has grown larger, not smaller, because frontier supply is being absorbed faster than it is produced.

...

### Spend Scorecard

| Spend Signal | Direction | Magnitude | Time Horizon |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GPU allocation pressure | Up | 70% of rack BOM concentrated in Rubin GPUs | Now through 2027 |
| Direct hardware availability | Tightening | Lead times likely to widen for frontier parts | 1 to 4 quarters |
| Power and interconnect spend | Up | Hundreds-of-MW site planning replacing mega-campus builds | 2 to 6 quarters |
| Secondary GPU pricing | Down | Older generations repricing lower as frontier demand diverges | Near term |

results.title: Cloud Infrastructure Strategy Shifts Due to Rising AI Costs
highlights: The early "more is more" phase of generative AI — more data, more models, more silicon — has collided with constrained hardware supply and rising compute costs, forcing AI service providers to raise prices and making in-house builds more expensive. With many organizations due for new cloud contracts, the question is no longer whether to expand infrastructure, but how to make it leaner. AI adoption has, per the outlet, exposed cracks in even the most robust hyperscaler foundations, and pressure on providers is now characterized by rising performance expectations, increasing workload complexity, and more decision makers in the room.

results.title: Compute Economics (GPU pricing, utilization, and the durability of a chip) — cere-bro
highlights:
The one-line state of knowledge as of 2026-08-14: compute has moved from a capacity market to a scarcity market, prices are being set by auction rather than by contract, and the incidence falls hardest on the smallest trainers.

...

## The current price regime (2026-08)

Three data points from the same week, which line up unusually cleanly:

- Nebius held its first auction of computing capacity in Q2 2026 and cleared Blackwell-generation capacity at "15% above the highest price we ever charged before" (CEO Arkady Volozh, earnings call, reported by The Information, 08-13). Nebius also said it is deliberately selling capacity closer to when customers need it, to capture the spot premium instead of locking it away in forward contracts. That is a supplier consciously converting a contract business into a spot business.
- Contract durations are collapsing and volumes are being rationed. Evan Morikawa of robotics-model startup Generalist talked to about 17 different AI cloud providers hunting compute, and reported that a year earlier he could get reasonable prices on contracts as short as one year; six months into that contract, needing roughly a thousand more chips, the market had changed (The Information, 08-13). His line, "it's like VC currency right now to know the current price of GPUs," is a market-microstructure observation: when the price of an input becomes private information, the input is scarce.
- Nvidia's market capitalization moved $1 trillion above Apple's over roughly two weeks, an 18% Nvidia rise against a ~10% Apple fall. Broad macro explains part of it; chip rental prices going "through the roof" is the part that belongs on this page.

Who pays. The incidence is not uniform. Hyperscalers hold forward contracts and their own capacity. The hardest-hit class is what The Information calls neolabs: startups training their own frontier or domain models, who need hundreds to thousands of chips, have finite venture funding, and cannot outbid a hyperscaler in an auction. The structural consequence is that a rising spot price does not slow frontier training, it slows independent frontier training, which is a concentration effect rather than a slowdown.

...

## 2026-09-25: the CPU shortage gets a mechanism, and China gets measured

- CPU shortage (Pragmatic Engineer): cloud CPU spot pricing has effectively vanished, server orders take about six months at 10% to 20% higher prices, and the datacenter CPU-to-GPU ratio moved from 1:8 to about 1:4 (possibly 1:1). Demand comes from RL environments and cloud-hosted agents running tools. Supply is squeezed by TSMC favoring GPUs and DRAM fabs favoring HBM. This gives the 09-10 CPU note its mechanism.
- SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model: China 24GW+ (vs US 56GW, EMEA ~14GW), ~50GW more in pipeline and announcements. BAT capex $20B in 2Q26, more than doubled, with negative free cash flow at all three for the first time. The opposite bottleneck to the West: buildings and power are abundant, chips are constrained.
- Deals: Anthropic and Akamai, seven years, $11.6B, with a warrant for up to 5% of Akamai; Anthropic's compute deals reach $517B in 11 months. DensityAI (ex-Tesla Dojo) nears a $10B valuation with a conditional AWS purchase agreement.

...

## 2026-10-18: rental prices up, neocloud stocks down

- B300 rental rates rose more than 20% in a month while Nebius, IREN and CoreWeave shares fell on fears GPUs depreciate too fast (investor commentary on X, 10-17; unsourced figure). Demand for open-model inference is cited as the driver, consistent with DeepSeek, Meta and Reflection all shipping open models this week.
- Ben Horowitz: Amazon's CEO told him AI compute is sold out "beyond 2028." Binding constraint is power, cooling and buildings, not GPUs.
- HSBC: custom AI chips reach 57% of HBM demand by 2028, with HBM growing from ~$64B (2026) to ~$280B (2028), so GPU HBM demand can still nearly triple.
- a16z co-led Volta's Series A, "the neocloud for Little Tech": cloud operations plus project finance so startups without financeable balance sheets can sign long-term capacity. The Information (10-17) reports a16z and General Catalyst racing to secure chips for portfolio companies.
- Tension: if compute is sold out to 2028 and rentals are rising, the market's depreciation fear is a financing story, not a demand story. Watch CoreWeave debt pricing.

## 2026-10-19: +50GW funded, neoclouds wobble

- SemiAnalysis forecasts +43 to +50GW of 2027 datacenter capacity on about $1T of binding 2026 leases and parabolic hyperscaler self-build starts; >24GW is in advanced construction at the top 40 campuses alone. Modular builds (AWS Project Houdini, DayOne ~9 months) and behind-the-meter power shorten timelines. Altimeter's Gerstner guessed 25GW (summary).
- Neocloud stress continues: Microsoft exits Nscale's UK site over power delays; Firmus pulled its IPO; CoreWeave and peers fell ~20% in a week; Nebius has 5 GW contracted but ~0.6 GW live (industry). Musk says SpaceX cannot rent inference compute.
- Meta's AMD co-design (1.5x over a direct port) makes multi-vendor training credible (summary).
- Shift: the shortage now splits by builder. Hyperscaler self-builds are on schedule; debt-funded neoclouds absorb power and timing risk. SemiAnalysis hints memory and logic become the 2027-28 constraint.

## 2026-10-20: glut and shortage at once

- Glut: Business Insider: Amazon has warehouses of uninstalled GPUs and an "early rack receipt" program taking ~$3B a month (roundup).
- Shortage: Nebius B200 spot reportedly >3x in a week; IREN says 2026 is sold out and contracts are >2x last year; Anthropic reportedly seeks another 460 MW at Nscale Monarch after a $45B 6-year deal.
- Reconciled: the constraint is powered floor space. Chips pile up where buildings lag; powered GPUs get scarce. Consistent with SemiAnalysis (10-19).
- Forecasts: Morgan Stanley $1.58T 2027 spend incl. leases (Nvidia ~$690B, 44%); Gartner $6T 2027-30 with >$3.5T at write-down risk; Goldman: CoreWeave ~15% unlevered IRR even at zero GPU residual.
- Utilization side: Meta Prometheus reports >85% pre-training goodput and 47-54K GPU-hour MTBI; GB300 only 5-10% faster than GB200 on Meta's mix.
- Memory decoupling: Marvell's photonic modules place HBM/DDR up to 50 m from the GPU at hundreds of ns.

## 2026-10-22: prices up at the GPU, down at the market

Industry roundup. DeepInfra raises GPU-hour prices from Nov 9 (A100 +67%, B200 +33%); Nebius B200 spot +55% in a day; AWS takes GB300 racks before it has power; SpaceX's compute-leasing segment hits $7.56B/quarter. Meanwhile SOX loses ~$2T over 8 sessions and CoreWeave falls 25% in a week. Anthropic's prospectus shows ~$9B H1 compute and $600B+ in commitments. SemiAnalysis: Ascend 950 ~A100-to-MI300X class; DSv4.1-Flash step gains only 1.32x from 2x compute. NVIDIA DSX POD: 6 months to 14 days onsite; Nscale MaxLPS +37% GPUs per power budget.

...

## 2026-10-26: rent rises on old cards; credit closes on neoclouds

- DeepInfra from Nov 9: A100 $0.89 to $1.49 (+67%), H100 $2.90, H200 $3.49, B200 $4.89, B300 $5.89; serverless token prices flat (summary).
- Penalties and supply: data center late fees $5M+/day; Nscale ~25K active of 461K contracted GPUs; transformers 160+ weeks; DRAM/SSD/ABF 2-5x normal lead times.
- Credit: Nvidia's AI-cloud exposure $171.5B; CoreWeave CDS ~1,082 bps; Musk says debt markets are "almost entirely shut off" for AI-only neoclouds.
- Price war: OpenAI discounts up to 90% to win Anthropic accounts (roundup). Tokens are getting cheaper while GPU-hours get dearer, squeezing resellers.

...

Physical scarcity vs capital wariness (summary): B300 rents +52% since May while neocloud stocks fell 46-75%; revenue per MW varies 3x; hyperscalers hold $3T+ in data-center commitments ($1.3T leases); Meta modeled at 26GW by 2030 with $171B annual depreciation (S&P outlook negative); Baseten raising ~$2B at up to $30B; OpenAI closed ~$11B of $30B.

results.title: GPU Supply and Demand in 2026: Structural Shortage Across HBM, Foundry, and Power | SpecForge
highlights:
On-demand GPU capacity is effectively sold out and even older-generation chips are renting at levels not seen since 2024, while Blackwell PRO SKUs carry 3-7 month lead times and new H100 80GB SXM cards list at $25,000-$35,000 [S1][S2][S3].

Unlike the 2021-2022 crypto-driven cycle, this shortage is structural: high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TSMC N3 wafer capacity, and hyperscaler power budgets are all constrained at once, with spot DRAM prices up roughly 8x since early 2025 [S1][S2].

...

HBM is the single largest chokepoint: AI accelerators cannot ship without it, and DRAM makers are reallocating wafer capacity from commodity DDR to HBM stacks, which has dragged spot DRAM pricing up by roughly 8x since early 2025 [S1].

Foundry supply is equally tight. TSMC N3 capacity, which underpins most current AI accelerators, is approaching full utilization through at least 2027, and new EUV-equipped fabs take years to come online [S1]. The implication for buyers is that any "supply catch-up" story has to clear HBM and N3 simultaneously, which is why [S2] reports lead times lengthening rather than easing as of March 2026.

Power is the third leg. Hyperscalers are signing multi-year infrastructure deals ahead of deployment, and competing AI labs (Anthropic and Google have both rented capacity from xAI) are partnering to secure compute rather than waiting for new silicon [S1]. For a spec-side view of how the cloud-rental side is responding, see the GPU price index 2026: cloud rental surge versus retail volatility tracking file.

...

## Price and Lead-Time Snapshot, March 2026

GPU supply and demand balance 2026 - Price and Lead-Time Snapshot, March 2026

Real-time sourcing data from March 2026 puts L20 48GB at $4,000-$4,100 (10-15 units), L40S 48GB at $8,610-$8,900 (20-70 units), RTX 5000 32GB at $4,500-$4,770, RTX 4000 Ada 20GB at $1,385-$1,420, RTX 6000 Ada 48GB at $7,400-$7,800, RTX PRO 4000 24GB at $2,000-$2,100, and RTX PRO 6000 96GB at $9,450-$9,800 [S2].

New H100 80GB SXM cards list at $25,000-$35,000 with used units at $18,000-$22,000, while A100 80GB is discontinued new and trades at $12,000-$18,000 used, and A100 40GB sits at $7,000-$10,000 used [S3]. Bulk H100 wait times shortened from 6+ months to 2-3 months through 2025, but Blackwell PRO lead times moved in the opposite direction, hitting 3-7 months by Q1 2026 [S2][S3].

Allocation is "highly unstable across distributors," so pricing is tied to allocation timing and ship-to location, with spot-market sourcing becoming the norm for tier-2 and tier-3 buyers [S2].

## Buying vs. Renting vs. Reselling: A Comparison

For a data-center buyer needing H100-class throughput today, renting on-demand is effectively sold out and older-generation rentals have re-rated to 2024 highs, so committed multi-year capacity (or a partner-hosted deal) is the only reliable path [S1][S2].

For a budget buyer who can tolerate Ampere, used A100 80GB at $12,000-$18,000 is the lowest-risk entry point, but expect 6-12 months of additional depreciation as Hopper and Blackwell expand [S3].

For consumer inference and fine-tuning, the RTX 4090 used market at $900-$1,400 (versus $1,600-$2,000 new) is the sweet spot, with the RTX 5090 launch in early 2025 still pulling 4090 prices down [S3].

For resellers and data-center liquidators, consumer GPUs lose 40-50% of value within 12 months of a successor launch, while data-center GPUs retain value longer thanks to AI demand but still drop 50-60% across a full generation transition [S3].

...

The cycle is structural, not speculative: AI demand is long-term and sustained, unlike the 2021-2022 crypto mining spike that unwound when coin economics flipped [S2]. Three things can break the logjam: a new HBM fab ramp (SK hynix, Micron, Samsung), TSMC N3 or N2 capacity easing, and incremental grid power for hyperscale campuses, and none of the three is on a 2026 timeline [S1].

Secondary-market risk is real. Data-center GPUs have often run at sustained compute load for months, so buyers should request serial numbers, runtime hours, thermal-throttling history, and RMA records, and run nvidia-smi plus a sustained memory test, because HBM errors can develop under heavy use and are not always immediately apparent [S3].

results.title: Dedicated GPU Cost for Machine Learning: 2026 Pricing Guide – ServerPronto University
highlights:
On-demand GPU pricing is the most straightforward model: you pay an hourly rate for exclusive access to hardware. According to Intuition Labs’ 2026 Data Center GPU Pricing Index, NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs range from $1.38 to $12.29 per hour depending on the provider. The variation reflects differences in infrastructure quality, geographic location, and service tier.

Major cloud providers charge varying hourly rates for H100 instances; boutique providers may offer lower GPU-hour rates. The trade-off is ecosystem maturity and support responsiveness.

NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the newer generation with superior memory bandwidth, start at approximately $2.50 per hour according to GMI Cloud’s 2026 GPU Cloud Pricing Comparison. For inference workloads that don’t require the absolute highest compute density, H200s often deliver better value than H100s when you factor in model size and latency requirements.

 Pro Tip On-demand pricing works best for short-term projects, experimentation, and workloads with ... Lock in hourly rates before scaling to production.

...

Spot instances offer 40-70% discounts but can be reclaimed with 2-5 minutes’ notice. They suit fault-tolerant workloads like distributed training with checkpointing and batch processing.

...

The hourly GPU rate captures only 30-40% of true infrastructure cost. Data egress fees, storage, CPU overhead, and networking add up quickly. According to Northflank’s 2026 TCO analysis, low hourly GPU rates can be offset by additional costs for CPU, storage, and networking, which may result in a higher total bill than an all-inclusive, higher-priced hourly option.

Egress fees for moving data out of the data center are often the biggest surprise. Transferring large checkpoints can incur costs; frequent iterations compound these costs.

...

CPU allocation varies by provider. Misaligned CPU-to-GPU ratios slow data loading and waste GPU compute time.

results.title: How Nvidia Is Trying to Solve the Data Center Power ...
highlights:
How Nvidia Is Trying to Solve the Data Center Power Bottleneck — The Information

# How Nvidia Is Trying to Solve the Data Center Power Bottleneck

By 

Phoebe Liu
